title: E40 - Lawyer Value in an AI World: Litigator, Coder & AI Evangelist Damien Riehl
author: Damien Riehl

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not address the cluster’s central concern that automation may disrupt associate training and expertise reproduction. Instead, it redirects attention to AI’s immediate business-model consequences, particularly client resistance to hourly billing when comparable work can be completed much faster with AI.
qs: So I think that law firms and law departments are, we'll start with the law firms, are really coming to grips with the business model.

Like these are all things that everyone's saying, how can we continue making money in an age where I can do things more quickly and my clients are telling me to do things more quickly and I can't really do time performance to be able to say, hey, this really took eight hours and the in-house council is using the same tools and saying, no, no, no, no, I did the same thing in about 20 minutes.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source provides no substantive claims, evidence or argument about user-led legal AI adoption, capability readiness, verification, market scenarios or skills. A podcast sign-off alone is insufficient to assess its position relative to the cluster synthesis.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account that AI pressures time-based pricing and may shift work toward in-house legal departments and lower-cost AI-first competitors. Its examples are illustrative and qualified rather than market-wide proof, and it does not materially address apprenticeship, verification or implementation constraints.
qs: Like these are all things that everyone's saying, how can we continue making money in an age where I can do things more quickly and my clients are telling me to do things more quickly and I can't really do time performance to be able to say, hey, this really took eight hours and the in-house council is using the same tools and saying, no, no, no, no, I did the same thing in about 20 minutes.
This is new world where the newest competitors, the biggest competitors of the law firm are their clients.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that in-house AI adoption can strengthen corporate legal departments as buyers and selectively substitute for outside counsel. It cites a case-specific transfer of substantial external spending in-house and frames clients as emerging competitors to law firms, while its own uncertainty and anecdotal basis do not establish universal outside-counsel decline.
qs: And by the way, that was going to be annually, they estimated about $5 to $6 million in external spend that they brought in-house and they look to expand that.
And you have to tell me what is the incremental value on top of what I can do in-house that you can't do.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: AI compresses document-production work while preserving lawyer value in trust, tacit judgment and accountability. It also aligns with the cluster’s expected hybrid pricing shift and buyer-side reallocation of work, while treating AI-first competition and demand growth as uncertain predictions rather than established market-wide effects.
qs: This is new world where the newest competitors, the biggest competitors of the law firm are their clients.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source modestly supports the cluster by identifying Clio as another aspiring legal-AI competitor beyond the most prominent specialist vendors, while explicitly leaving its success and durable value capture unresolved. It provides corporate and financing context, not evidence that Clio will succeed or that the market will remain fragmented.
qs: They've since raised a new round of financing, and they are going to try to be one of the key players in the AI for legal market.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Riehl supports the cluster’s core view that AI will redesign and compress component tasks rather than simply eliminate legal practice, while shifting lawyers’ defensible value toward judgment, advocacy, relationships and accountability. He also aligns with the cluster’s qualified market analysis: AI pressures hourly billing and encourages fixed fees and insourcing, but does not dictate the billable hour’s disappearance. His agentic and automated-dispute-resolution scenarios are prospective and less attentive to verification and implementation constraints, but do not displace his overall support.
qs: So even litigation, which I think is going to be safe for a while, still has aspects of my job's going to change.
So I think that people talk about the death of the bill of blower is just, that's the wrong framing.

kp.k: AI pressures pricing without necessarily ending hourly billing
kp.d: Riehl frames 2026 as a business-model reckoning after awareness in 2023–2024 and adoption in 2025. He predicts successful firms will expand flat, subscription or success fees while retaining hourly billing for uncertain work. His illustrative progression is from 10% alternative-fee revenue to 20%, 40% and perhaps 60–70%, citing accounting firms' asserted 60–70% flat-fee share as an analogy rather than presenting study evidence. Lower AI-enabled delivery costs could increase margins under fixed fees.
qs: So I think that the nub of all of the hand bringing within law firms goes to the business model.
It's not going to die.
I'm going to press down my costs for those, which will then increase my profit margins.

kp.k: Profitability gains depend on monetising distinctive expertise
kp.d: Riehl predicts higher earnings for some lawyers, not the profession uniformly. He argues that clients buy trust and tacit knowledge absent from contracts, cases and knowledge-management artifacts, rather than document production or elapsed time. His hypothetical AmLaw 20 lawyer charges $10,000 for advice produced in 20 minutes because its distinctive insights remain valuable. He doubts large institutions' willingness to move away from hourly billing.
qs: But we don't sell widgets because AI is cranking those widgets out. We sell trust.
So I think that decoupling time from value is where the winners are going to be.
I would say some lawyers are going to make significantly more.
And it took me 20 minutes to be able to write up this thing for $10,000.

kp.k: Client adoption changes firms' incentives to embrace AI
kp.d: Riehl attributes slow adoption to professional inertia and hourly incentives, drawing an analogy with technology-aided document review: firms resist paying for tools that reduce billable work. He distinguishes AI from that earlier transition because in-house lawyers now use the tools themselves and can challenge outside counsel's claimed effort and incremental value. This is his explanation of the 2023–2026 transition, not a measured adoption study.
qs: I would say it's inertia and the overcoming of inertia.
So why would you spend money on a technology that makes you less money?
But in the new world, with AI, in-house council are using this all the time.
This is new world where the newest competitors, the biggest competitors of the law firm are their clients.

kp.k: Salesforce savings illustrate reported insourcing of external work
kp.d: Riehl recounts a Salesforce representative saying on stage that between January and July 2025, approximately $3 million previously spent externally was saved by bringing work in-house using tools such as Vincent. He subsequently describes this as the first six months and reports an annual estimate of about $5–$6 million, with expansion intended. These are customer claims relayed by a vendor-affiliated guest, with his express uncertainty, rather than independently established savings.
qs: I was on stage with Salesforce and Salesforce said that in 25, between January and July, I think they saved $3 million that they used to spend external spend that they brought in-house because they used tools like Vincent and others.
And by the way, that was going to be annually, they estimated about $5 to $6 million in external spend that they brought in-house and they look to expand that.

kp.k: In-house buyers may adopt faster than law firms
kp.d: Abramowitz says in-house adoption has exceeded his earlier expectation that firms would be the principal AI buyers. Reporting a point made in connection with Sandstone, in which he has invested, he contrasts firms' preference for bespoke differentiation and building with corporate departments' readiness to buy. He also identifies pressure from CIOs, COOs and CFOs expecting productivity gains in legal and other back-office functions. Riehl agrees, illustrating how a direct AI query might replace instructing external counsel and waiting days for advice costing $10,000.
qs: What I would not have expected is that in-house counsel would have been a little bit farther ahead on the adoption.
They're much more likely to want to build than to buy.
Like I think we're now seeing in-house potentially be the more interested buyer of AI than even the law firms.
That number one lawyer, option one lawyer doesn't know why the phone stops ringing.

kp.k: Tacit intuition may become quantifiable data
kp.d: Abramowitz uses baseball analytics to suggest that widely available AI information could make experienced judgment the remaining differentiator. Riehl qualifies this argument: apparent gut instinct may itself consist of observations not yet collected or quantified. His 80% and 90% deal-outcome examples are hypothetical illustrations, not empirical findings, and suggest that today's tacit advantage need not remain permanently outside AI's reach.
qs: And that something is just data that we haven't yet quantified.

And if you quantify that data, then it turns from magical stuff intuition that somebody has as gut instinct into a data point that we could be able to say, you know, 80% of the deals, 90% of the deals go this way, because of that data point that we thought was intuition, but it's something actually countable.

kp.k: Human-facing tasks persist within otherwise transformed practices
kp.d: Riehl expects courtroom advocacy and interpersonal negotiation to retain a human role, but cautions against treating whole practice areas as protected. Drawing on over 15 years as a litigator, he says court appearances occupied little of his work; client communications and written outputs are more exposed. For transactions, he imagines privacy-preserving agents negotiating parties' thresholds, resolving 90% of issues and leaving 10% for face-to-face discussion. This is a prospective task-level scenario.
qs: So I would say the litigation is probably safe. But the real question is for which tasks?
But I, as a litigator for over 15 years, very rarely stood in front of a judge or stood in front of a jury.
And if the bot in a very privacy-centric way says we have agreement on 90% of the things, here's the 10% where we hammer out face-to-face.

kp.k: Cheaper legal work need not increase transaction volume
kp.d: Abramowitz questions a straightforward Jevons-paradox prediction for M&A: legal expense may not be the binding constraint because transactions are difficult more generally. He asks whether lawyers could shift from documenting risks to improving transaction effectiveness, while acknowledging that this might instead be management consultants' role. This is the host's exploratory argument, not evidence of realised demand expansion.
qs: But the reason that you don't do more M&A is not because it's so expensive from a legal perspective. It's because M&A is so challenging just in general.
So the question is, is that actually focused on creating an effective transaction?

kp.k: Litigation automation could reshape dispute volume and prevention
kp.d: Riehl says he and others are building plaintiff, defence, court and arbitrator bots. He argues that lower litigation costs increase dispute volume and strain already overwhelmed courts. Referring to a prospective American Arbitration Association workflow producing an outcome 20 minutes after document uploads, he speculates that sufficiently cheap dispute resolution could reduce willingness to pay for M&A diligence intended to avoid litigation. No measured volume or cost results support this scenario in the transcript.
qs: That is shrinking the cost of litigation, which is then increasing the volume of litigation, which is overwhelming and already overwhelmed courts.
And so we're also building court bots and arbitrator bots to be able to deal with that increased volume.
So if litigation decreases in cost, maybe the price I spend on due diligence and the stuff to avoid that litigation risk, maybe I spend less on that.

kp.k: Firm reputation may outlast diligence's time-spent signal
kp.d: Abramowitz asks whether AI undermines a diligence memo's signal that lawyers slowed down and scrutinised a transaction. Riehl counters that prestigious letterhead and perceived risk transfer may matter more than time or even content: the legal department pays partly to place responsibility with an established firm. Their exchange distinguishes process-signalling from reputational assurance rather than establishing either empirically.
qs: Will the psychology always require work? And then what does that work actually become?
That CYA aspect that we hired this AMLAW20 firm, their letterhead is on this memo.
Therefore, I've shifted my risk from the law department to the law firm. So the letterhead is really what you're paying for.

kp.k: AI-first boutiques could challenge incumbent infrastructure and pricing
kp.d: Both speakers anticipate experienced lawyers leaving large firms to offer cheaper flat-fee services with AI-enabled infrastructure. Abramowitz says his presentations on AI-first law firms provoke more incumbent attention than discussion of software vendors. He predicts departures could target major transactions, not merely smaller work or improved work-life balance, and questions whether startup-style capital raising is necessary. His evidence consists of presentation reactions and conversations with lawyers considering departures, not demonstrated market displacement.
qs: I'm the same person I was 20 minutes ago before I jumped ship. I'm gonna charge you less money and flat fees.
Whether or not this ends up being a trend, what I can tell you it absolutely has done is get law firms to pay attention, right?
Like I'm not even sure if you even need that capital.
I just don't think you necessarily need the old infrastructure of a law firm to service that kind of deal.

kp.k: Ownership and accreditation changes are framed as entry threats
kp.d: Riehl asserts that Arizona alternative business structures can practise across all 50 states through routes an ethics-lawyer acquaintance advises on, and identifies venture capital and private equity as potential funding sources. He further asserts that Texas and Florida no longer require ABA accreditation, then imagines a six-month AI-first law school and practice under an Arizona ABS. These are his regulatory assertions and speculative training scenario; the transcript supplies neither governing rules nor the conditions for those pathways. Abramowitz analogises investor interest to private equity's entry into medical practices over the preceding 20 years.
qs: And the fact that an Arizona ABS can practice law in all 50 states.
And let me add one more piece to this beyond Arizona is Texas and Florida saying that ABA accreditation is no longer necessary to practice law in Texas and in Florida.
And maybe I don't spend three years, but I spend six months learning this AI first work.

kp.k: Relationships and human qualities become strategic differentiators
kp.d: Abramowitz recommends considering whether offices could attract clients for more in-person contact rather than simply reducing space. Riehl agrees, arguing that personal interaction supports advocacy, negotiations and client acquisition as AI produces more written work. He reports Jordan Furlong's three enduring human attributes as trust, intuition and integrity, including real-time courtroom judgment and counterparties' confidence in a lawyer's conduct. These are strategic judgments rather than comparative performance findings.
qs: How do we get our clients coming back to our law firm office?
So I think you're on to something that in real life is going to be the key of the kingdom as AI is doing a lot of the other things.
Jordan Furlong wrote a great sub stack piece about the three attributes of humanity that are going to matter going forward for lawyers.
So between those three, trust, integrity, and intuition, those are probably the aspects of the humanity that are going to remain.

kp.k: Current legal data is presented as a competitive barrier
kp.d: Riehl argues that litigation, regulatory, advisory and bankruptcy work require current cases, statutes and regulations, including changes that invalidate older authorities. He contrasts this with deal work, where transaction execution may be more central. From his Clio position, he asserts that only three companies possess the relevant US legal materials and that general AI providers lack them. He also speculates that diversified incumbents may favour profits or tax-and-accounting investment over legal R&D. These are vendor-positioned market claims, not independently documented comparisons.
qs: I would say the hyperscaler whippersnappers, what they don't have is yesterday's case, and yesterday's statute, and yesterday's regulation.
And so only three companies in the world have that in the US.
But it's important to know that yesterday's case overruled the two years ago case.
So maybe I just divert my law R&D to my tax and accounting law, R&D, because it turns out tax and accounting, accountants pay for software.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Damien Riehl predicts a redistribution of legal work and profits: AI commoditises document production and routine advice, while rewarding firms that sell distinctive expertise, adopt flat fees and preserve human relationships.
pts.d: Riehl makes the following claims and predictions. (1) The billable hour will survive, but successful firms will increase their flat-fee or other non-hourly revenue and use AI to lower delivery costs and increase margins. His illustrative trajectory moves from 10% non-hourly revenue toward 50–70%; this is not presented as a measured forecast. Some lawyers will earn significantly more, while others will earn less. (2) Lawyers' distinctive value lies in trust and knowledge not already captured in contracts, legal sources or knowledge-management systems. Decoupling that value from time could allow experienced lawyers to serve more clients and increase aggregate earnings. He also qualifies the durability of tacit expertise: some intuition is uncollected data that could eventually be quantified. (3) AI-using legal departments become competitors to their outside firms. Routine research, compliance questions and contract insights can move in-house, leaving external lawyers to justify the incremental expertise they provide. His Vincent example describes obtaining multi-jurisdictional legal answers in seconds or minutes instead of commissioning days of outside work. (4) AI adoption was slowed by inertia and hourly-billing incentives; client use of the same tools makes continued resistance more difficult. (5) Human-facing litigation tasks are comparatively protected, but litigation as a whole is not insulated: drafting and other preparatory tasks change. In transactions, he envisages privacy-sensitive agent-to-agent negotiation resolving most issues before humans negotiate the remainder. (6) Riehl says plaintiff and defence bots lower litigation costs and increase volume, generating demand for court and arbitration bots. He further speculates that much cheaper dispute resolution could reduce clients' willingness to spend on diligence intended to avoid litigation. (7) A major firm's letterhead can supply risk transfer independently of time spent producing a memo. Nevertheless, experienced lawyers could leave incumbent firms and provide lower-priced flat-fee services through AI-first boutiques. (8) Riehl identifies Arizona alternative business structures, outside investment and potential changes to educational accreditation requirements as interacting sources of competitive disruption. He asserts that Arizona ABSs can practise across all 50 states and imagines a shorter AI-first educational pathway; these are his regulatory assertions and hypothetical scenario, not independently established findings here. (9) He expects in-person relationships and rainmaking to become more important relative to document-drafting skill, and endorses trust, intuition and integrity as durable human attributes. (10) In the legal-technology market, he argues that access to current cases, statutes and regulations protects specialist providers against hyperscalers, particularly in litigation, advisory, regulatory and bankruptcy work. He claims Clio combines that content advantage with stronger innovation incentives and AI-assisted engineering capable of dramatically shortening development cycles.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Riehl relies primarily on business-model reasoning, professional and product-development experience, reported customer savings, historical analogy and cited professional authority, rather than systematic benchmarks.
pts.d: For pricing and adoption, Riehl uses the historical analogy of technology-assisted review: firms previously earned substantial document-review revenue from associates, so technology that reduced hours conflicted with their billing incentives. He also invokes the Big Four's accounting fee mix as a business-model comparison, asserting that 60–70% is flat fee without supplying underlying data. For in-house substitution, he reports that Salesforce described approximately $3 million in external spending brought in-house between January and July 2025 using Vincent and other tools, with an estimated annual total of $5–6 million. This is a customer account relayed by Riehl, not independently verified savings or evidence of an industry-wide effect. His hypothetical $10,000 advice produced in 20 minutes illustrates the economics of value-based pricing; it is not an observed pricing study. His argument about litigation tasks draws on more than 15 years as a litigator, during which he says courtroom appearances occupied little of his time. For automated disputes, he describes his own involvement in building plaintiff, defence, court and arbitrator bots; he also invokes an American Arbitration Association example to illustrate a prospective rapid document-to-outcome workflow. No litigation-cost or caseload measurements are supplied. His ABS argument draws on an ethics lawyer's work identifying routes for Arizona ABSs to operate nationally, without setting out those routes or their conditions. His account of durable human attributes expressly endorses an argument he credits to Jordan Furlong; it is not presented as an empirical finding. His claims about Clio's engineering speed and advantages over competitors draw on his experience working at Clio and other legal-technology companies. The claimed 10x or 100x acceleration and year-to-20-minute comparison are anecdotal estimates, not controlled engineering measurements. His assertions about legal-content concentration and competitors' R&D incentives are market arguments, with no supporting market dataset. The episode supplies no model benchmarks, measured hallucination rates or systematic assessment of the verification work required before relying on the rapid legal answers described.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview frames 2026 as a business-model transition following 2025 adoption; most market outcomes remain conditional predictions without firm dates.
pts.d: Riehl characterises 2023 as uncertainty, 2024 as awakening, 2025 as engagement and 2026 as the point at which firms must decide what to do about their business models. His explanation is overcoming inertia rather than a specified benchmark breakthrough. The Salesforce account concerns January–July 2025, although he subsequently describes it as the first six months; the $5–6 million amount is an annual estimate, not a separately reported realised result. Higher profits are conditional on changing pricing, lowering costs and selling expertise the client does not already possess. He explicitly limits the prediction to some lawyers and doubts large AmLaw 20 institutions' willingness to make the transition. Hourly billing remains appropriate for some uncertain work; he does not forecast its complete disappearance. In-house substitution is described as already occurring, but its extent depends on how much work can be answered from available legal and contractual materials and how much requires additional human expertise. Human courtroom participation is expected to remain for the speakers' lifetimes, expressly qualified by hope; the broader claim that litigation is safe is narrowed to particular tasks and to 'a while.' Agent-to-agent negotiation and very cheap automated dispute resolution are prospective scenarios with no implementation timetable. Lower diligence expenditure is expressly contingent on litigation becoming much cheaper, not an unconditional forecast of reduced M&A legal demand. The shorter AI-first law-school example is hypothetical and tied to Riehl's assertions about Texas and Florida accreditation changes and Arizona ABS structures; the transcript does not establish that the imagined six-month route is available. Specialist legal-content advantages persist in his argument unless hyperscalers obtain sufficiently current law. AI-assisted engineering acceleration is described as a present capability relative to work approximately five years earlier. His endorsement of durable intuition coexists with his suggestion that some currently tacit judgment may become quantifiable.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects differ across outside firms, experienced lawyers, corporate buyers, litigators, transactional teams, courts, new legal-service entrants and software providers.
pts.d: Large incumbent law firms, particularly AmLaw 20 firms and the Kirkland examples, face pressure on hourly revenue and routine advisory work, but could increase margins under non-hourly pricing. Experienced lawyers with distinctive knowledge, trusted relationships and client-development ability could capture more value, serve more clients or leave for lower-overhead AI-first boutiques; lawyers who fail to adapt could lose work and income. Associates feature in the historical account of labour-intensive review and current research workflows, but Riehl does not supply a quantified junior-employment forecast. Corporate legal departments are the buyer-side beneficiaries of faster internal answers and reduced external spending; outside counsel must demonstrate value beyond those internal capabilities. Litigation lawyers retain a human role in courtroom advocacy and client contact while other tasks are automated. Transactional lawyers could spend less time negotiating routine issues and more time resolving the difficult remainder, while diligence providers could face lower demand if litigation risk becomes cheaper to bear. Litigants may face lower dispute costs, whereas already burdened courts may receive greater volumes and turn toward automation. These are litigation-cost and institutional-capacity claims, not a quantified claim about closing the civil justice gap. AI-first boutiques and Arizona ABS legal-service businesses could compete with incumbents and draw venture-capital or private-equity backing; these providers are distinct from software vendors. Prospective lawyers and established professionals could be affected by the imagined weakening of educational entry barriers. Judges, juries, opposing counsel and clients remain audiences for human trust, integrity and persuasion. In the vendor market, Clio and other specialist legal-content owners are positioned by Riehl against hyperscalers that lack current legal sources, while engineers may gain faster AI-assisted software-development capabilities.
